Module 10
Impressionism (Monet): Landscape Painting
Instructional Page
👀 START HERE · LOOK FIRST
Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872 A.D. Public domain.

Look for one minute before you read on. Notice the dashes of orange on the water, the soft blue haze, and how the harbor is suggested rather than drawn in sharp detail.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How do you paint light, weather, and a passing moment instead of every tiny detail?
The painting above gave a whole movement its name: Impressionism. Claude Monet and other artists stopped hiding their brushstrokes and started painting the way light actually looks in a single moment. Today you learn how they used color, texture, value, movement, and rhythm to do it, so you can paint your own landscape the same way next week.
✅ BY THE END OF THIS MODULE, YOU WILL BE ABLE TO
☐ Explain how Monet and the Impressionists used broken color and short brushstrokes to capture a single moment of light.
☐ Use the five art tools, color, texture, value, movement, and rhythm, to describe an Impressionist painting.
☐ Plan and paint an original landscape with a foreground, middle ground, and background using Impressionist brushwork.
☐ Reflect on how light affects a finished piece of art.
📚 PART 1 · A NEW WAY OF PAINTING

The Salon set the rules

In the 1800s A.D., a powerful art show in France called the Salon decided which art was considered good. Paintings were expected to look smooth and realistic, with hidden brushstrokes and serious subjects like history or myth. Looser, more colorful work was often turned away.

Monet painted what he saw

Claude Monet and other artists wanted to paint light, weather, and everyday life. In 1874 A.D. they held their own show in Paris. Monet had a harbor painting in it titled Impression, Sunrise (the work above). A critic mocked it, saying it looked like just an impression and not a finished painting. The artists kept the name, and Impressionism was born.

💡 THE BIG IDEA
Impressionists believed a painting could capture a moment, the way light fell right then, instead of copying every detail exactly. Visible brushstrokes and bright color were the point, not a mistake.
⚡ QUICK CHECK-IN
Look back at Impression, Sunrise. What pulls your eye first? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)
🎨 PART 2 · FIVE TOOLS THAT MAKE IT WORK

Impressionists leaned on five tools again and again. Keep these in mind as you look at the paintings below and as you plan your own.

Color
Pure dabs of color placed side by side. Your eye mixes them. This is called broken color.
Texture
Short, thick brushstrokes you can almost feel. The paint surface is rough, not smooth.
Value
Lights and darks. Highlights and shadows show where the light is coming from.
Movement
Strokes that lead your eye across the scene, like water or wind in motion.
Rhythm
Marks that repeat with a beat, like the row of dashes in the sun's reflection.
👁 PART 3 · LOOK CLOSELY: ONE SUBJECT, TWO LIGHTS

Monet's Haystacks

Monet painted the same haystacks over and over at different times of day. The subject barely changes. The light changes everything. Compare these two paintings from the same series.

Claude Monet, Haystacks (End of Summer), 1890-1891 A.D. Public domain.
Soft daylight. Cool lavender field, gentle warm hills. The mood is calm and quiet.
Claude Monet, Grainstack (Sunset), 1890-1891 A.D. Public domain.
Sunset light. A blazing orange sky and a haystack glowing red and violet. The mood is warm and dramatic.
🔍 FIND THE FIVE TOOLS
Color in the dabs of orange, violet, and blue placed side by side. Texture in the thick, choppy strokes. Value in the bright sky against the dark stack. Movement in the strokes that sweep across the sky. Rhythm in the repeated short marks that build the field.
📚 PART 4 · PAINTING WATER AND REFLECTIONS

Monet's water gardens

Later in life Monet painted his own water garden again and again. In Water Lily Pond, a green footbridge arches over a pond crowded with lilies, and willow leaves drape from above. In Blue Water Lilies, he zooms in so far that the bridge disappears and the whole surface becomes a woven field of blue, with pale blossoms floating on top. Notice how the short strokes make the water feel like it is gently moving.

Claude Monet, Water Lily Pond, 1900 A.D. Public domain.
Claude Monet, Blue Water Lilies, 1916-1919 A.D. Public domain.
⚡ TRY IT · THINK LIKE AN IMPRESSIONIST
Read each one and pick the best match. Tap an answer to check it.
1. Monet painted the same haystacks over and over at different times of day. What was he mainly trying to capture?
2. In the sunset haystack, Monet puts small dabs of orange right next to dabs of violet so your eye blends them. What is this called?
3. In Impression, Sunrise, the sun's reflection is a column of repeated orange dashes with a steady beat. Which Principle is that?

💪 BEFORE YOU MOVE ON

Monet showed that a painting does not have to copy every detail to feel true. By choosing color, texture, value, movement, and rhythm on purpose, you can paint the way light feels in a single moment. Next week, you will do exactly that.
